q: Where did the earliest kind of print technology first develop?
o: Europe and Africa
China, Japan and Korea
India and Persia
North and South America
e: The earliest kind of print technology was developed in China, Japan and Korea as a system of hand printing.

q: Which is the oldest Japanese book printed in AD 868?
o: Ukiyo
Diamond Sutra
Gutenberg Bible
Amar Jiban
e: The oldest Japanese book, printed in AD 868, is the Buddhist Diamond Sutra, containing six sheets of text and woodcut illustrations.

q: Who brought the knowledge of woodblock printing from China back to Italy in 1295?
o: Johann Gutenberg
Marco Polo
Martin Luther
Christopher Columbus
e: In 1295, Marco Polo, a great explorer, returned to Italy after many years of exploration in China and brought the knowledge of woodblock printing back with him.

q: Who developed the first-known mechanical printing press in Strasbourg, Germany in the 1430s?
o: Johann Gutenberg
Richard M. Hoe
James Augustus Hickey
Erasmus
e: Johann Gutenberg developed the first-known printing press in Strasbourg, Germany in the 1430s and perfected the system by 1448.

q: Which was the first book printed by Johann Gutenberg on his printing press?
o: The Iliad
The Bible
Ninety-Five Theses
The Ramcharitmanas
e: Gutenberg perfected the system by 1448, and the first book he printed was the Bible (about 180 copies, taking three years to produce).

q: Who wrote the "Ninety-Five Theses" in 1517 criticising many practices and rituals of the Roman Catholic Church?
o: Menocchio
Martin Luther
Erasmus
Voltaire
e: In 1517, the religious reformer Martin Luther wrote Ninety-Five Theses criticising practices of the Roman Catholic Church, triggering the Protestant Reformation.

q: Who said, "Printing is the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one"?
o: Louise-Sebastien Mercier
Martin Luther
Mahatma Gandhi
Johann Gutenberg
e: Deeply grateful to print after his German New Testament sold 5,000 copies within weeks, Martin Luther declared, "Printing is the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one."

q: Who was "Menocchio", executed by the Roman Catholic Church in the 16th century?
o: A German goldsmith
A miller in Italy who read books and reinterpreted the message of the Bible
A French novelist
An English chapman
e: In the 16th century, Menocchio, a miller in Italy, began reading books available in his locality and reinterpreted the Bible; he was hauled up twice by the Inquisition and executed.

q: In which year did the Roman Catholic Church begin maintaining an "Index of Prohibited Books"?
e: Troubled by heretical readings like Menocchio's, the Roman Church imposed severe controls over publishers and booksellers and began maintaining an Index of Prohibited Books from 1558.

q: Who brought the first printing press to India (Goa) in the mid-16th century?
o: British merchants
Portuguese missionaries
Dutch traders
French East India Company
e: The printing press first came to Goa with Portuguese missionaries in the mid-sixteenth century (1556).

q: Who began to edit the "Bengal Gazette" from 1780, India's first weekly English magazine?
o: Gangadhar Bhattacharya
James Augustus Hickey
Warren Hastings
Raja Rammohun Roy
e: From 1780, James Augustus Hickey began to edit the Bengal Gazette, a weekly magazine that described itself as "a commercial paper open to all, but influenced by none".

q: Who published the Bengali weekly newspaper "Sambad Kaumudi" from 1821?
o: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
Rammohun Roy
Jyotiba Phule
Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar
e: Rammohun Roy published the Sambad Kaumudi from 1821, and the Hindu orthodoxy commissioned the Samachar Chandrika to oppose his reformist opinions.

q: Who wrote the autobiography "Amar Jiban", published in 1876 as the first full-length autobiography in Bengali?
o: Kailashbashini Debi
Rashsundari Debi
Tarabai Shinde
Pandita Ramabai
e: In East Bengal in the early 19th century, Rashsundari Debi, a young married girl in a very orthodox household, learnt to read in the secrecy of her kitchen and wrote her autobiography Amar Jiban, published in 1876.

q: Who wrote "Gulamgiri" (1871) about the injustices of the caste system?
o: Dr B. R. Ambedkar
Jyotiba Phule
Kashibaba
Periyar E. V. Ramaswamy
e: Jyotiba Phule, the Maratha pioneer of "low caste" protest movements, wrote about the injustices of the caste system in his Gulamgiri (1871).

q: In which year was the Vernacular Press Act passed to repress Indian-language newspapers?
e: In 1878, the Vernacular Press Act was passed, modelled on the Irish Press Laws, giving the colonial government extensive rights to censor reports and editorials in the vernacular press.

q: What were "Chapbooks" in 18th-century England?
o: Expensive leather-bound Latin Bibles
Pocket-sized books sold for a penny by travelling pedlars known as chapmen
Government tax registers
Monthly scientific encyclopedias
e: In England, penny chapbooks were carried by petty pedlars known as chapmen, and sold for a penny, so that even the poor could buy them.

q: What was "Bibliothèque Bleue" in France?
o: Royal library inside Versailles
Low-priced small books printed on poor quality paper and bound in cheap blue covers
Martin Luther's translation of the Bible
Official French royal gazette
e: In France, the "Biliothèque Bleue" were low-priced small books printed on poor quality paper and bound in cheap blue covers for wide popular reading.

q: What does "Vellum" refer to in pre-print European manuscript production?
o: Tree bark from China
A parchment made from the skin of animals
Inked wooden blocks
Metal movable lead mould
e: Luxury editions in pre-print Europe were still handwritten on very expensive vellum — a parchment made from the skin of animals — meant for aristocratic circles and rich monastic libraries.

q: What was the traditional Chinese "accordion book" folded and stitched at the side?
o: Printed on stone slabs
Thin, porous paper printed on only one side and then folded and stitched at the side
Written with gold ink on silk only
Printed using metal rotary cylinders
e: As both sides of the thin, porous sheet could not be printed in early China, the traditional Chinese "accordion book" was folded and stitched at the side.

q: Who was the Kanpur millworker who wrote and published "Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal" in 1938?
o: Sudarshan Chakr
Kashibaba
Jyotiba Phule
Ram Chaddha
e: Kashibaba, a Kanpur millworker, wrote and published Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal in 1938 to show the links between caste and class exploitation.

q: In 1907, Balgangadhar Tilak wrote with great sympathy about deported Punjab revolutionaries in which Marathi newspaper, leading to his imprisonment in 1908?
o: Harijan
Kesari
Sambad Kaumudi
Bengal Gazette
e: When Punjab revolutionaries were deported in 1907, Balgangadhar Tilak wrote with great sympathy about them in his Kesari, which led to his imprisonment in 1908 and widespread protests.

q: What was "Ukiyo" associated with famous Japanese artist Kitagawa Utamaro?
o: An ancient military law
An art form meaning "pictures of the floating world" depicting ordinary human experiences, especially urban ones
A type of European printing ink
A Buddhist monastery in Tibet
e: Kitagawa Utamaro, born in Edo in 1753, was widely known for his contributions to an art form called "ukiyo" ("pictures of the floating world") depicting ordinary urban experiences.

q: Who was the 18th-century French novelist who declared: "The printing press is the most powerful engine of progress and public opinion is the force that will sweep despotism away"?
o: Voltaire
Louise-Sebastien Mercier
Jean Jacques Rousseau
Montesquieu
e: Louise-Sebastien Mercier, a novelist in 18th-century France, proclaimed: "Tremble, therefore, tyrants of the world! Tremble before the virtual writer!"

q: Where was the first Tamil book printed by Catholic priests in 1579?
o: Madras
Cochin
Goa
Calcutta
e: Catholic priests printed the first Tamil book in 1579 at Cochin, and in 1713 the first Malayalam book was printed by them.

q: Which Persian newspapers began publication from India in 1822?
o: Jam-i-Jahan Nama and Shamsul Akhbar
Kesari and Maratha
Sambad Kaumudi and Samachar Chandrika
Al-Hilal and Comrade
e: From 1822, two Persian newspapers were published — Jam-i-Jahan Nama and Shamsul Akhbar — and in the same year a Gujarati newspaper, the Bombay Samachar, appeared.

q: Which Muslim seminary founded in 1867 published thousands upon thousands of fatwas guiding Muslims on everyday conduct and Islamic doctrines?
o: Aligarh College
Deoband Seminary
Fort William College
Jamia Millia
e: The Deoband Seminary, founded in 1867, published thousands upon thousands of fatwas telling Muslim readers how to conduct themselves in their everyday lives and explaining the meanings of Islamic doctrines.

q: In which city was the first printed edition of Tulsidas's "Ramcharitmanas" (a 16th-century text) published in 1810?
o: Lucknow
Calcutta
Bombay
Varanasi
e: The first printed edition of the Ramcharitmanas of Tulsidas, a sixteenth-century text, came out from Calcutta in 1810.

q: Who brought out the first Indian newspaper, also titled "Bengal Gazette"?
o: Rammohun Roy
Gangadhar Bhattacharya
Dwarkanath Tagore
Bal Gangadhar Tilak
e: By the close of the 18th century, Indians too began to publish Indian newspapers; the first to appear was the weekly Bengal Gazette brought out by Gangadhar Bhattacharya, who was close to Rammohun Roy.

q: Which two prominent women writers of 1880s Maharashtra wrote passionately about the miserable lives of upper-caste Hindu women, especially widows?
o: Rashsundari Debi and Kailashbashini Debi
Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai
Rokeya Hossein and Sarojini Naidu
Jane Austen and George Eliot
e: In the 1880s, in present-day Maharashtra, Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai wrote with passionate anger about the miserable lives of upper-caste Hindu women, especially widows.

q: What is "Calligraphy" (खुशनवीसी)?
o: Mechanical printing using metal blocks
The art of beautiful and stylised writing
Carving illustrations on copper
Censoring forbidden books
e: NCERT defines "Calligraphy" as the art of beautiful and stylised writing, crafted by skilled scribes in imperial China and Islamic/Indian manuscript traditions.

q: For a very long time in imperial China, who was the major producer of printed material and why?
o: Private newspaper barons for commercial ads
The imperial state, because it possessed a huge bureaucratic system recruiting personnel through civil service examinations for which textbooks were printed in vast numbers
Buddhist merchants in Japan
French Jesuit priests
e: The imperial state in China was for a very long time the major producer of printed material because its huge bureaucratic system recruited personnel through civil service examinations, requiring textbooks printed under imperial sponsorship.

q: Which Chinese city became the hub of the new print culture in the late 19th century, catering to Western-style schools as mechanical presses were imported?
o: Beijing
Shanghai
Canton
Nanjing
e: Western printing techniques and mechanical presses were imported in the late 19th century as Western powers established outposts in China; Shanghai became the hub of the new print culture.

q: Which two natural presses helped Johann Gutenberg design his mechanical printing press?
o: Steam locomotive and cotton gin
Olive press and wine press (plus his goldsmith expertise in lead moulds)
Spinning Jenny and water wheel
Clock gears and windmill
e: Having grown up on a large agricultural estate seeing wine and olive presses, and having mastered stone polishing, goldsmithing and lead moulds, Gutenberg adapted the olive press as the model for the printing press and moulds for casting metal types.

q: How fast could Gutenberg's printing press print sheets in his era?
o: 25 sheets per hour
250 sheets on one side per hour
8,000 sheets per hour
2,500 sheets per day
e: In Gutenberg's printing press, a long handle was attached to the screw to press down the platen over the printing block resting on damp paper; it could print 250 sheets on one side per hour.

q: Why did early printed books in Europe still closely resemble written manuscripts in appearance and layout?
o: Because metal letters imitated ornamental handwritten styles, borders were illuminated by hand with foliage, and spaces for decoration were left blank for buyers to choose painters
Because printing presses could only print blank boxes
Because ink came only in gold
Because Gutenberg banned decorative borders
e: Even though books were printed mechanically, the metal letters imitated ornamental handwritten styles; borders were illuminated by hand with foliage and illustrations painted, and buyers chose designs and painting schools.

q: Who was Richard M. Hoe of New York and what major technical innovation did he perfect by the mid-19th century?
o: Woodblock ink in Edo
The power-driven cylindrical press capable of printing 8,000 sheets per hour
The offset six-colour press
The paperback Shilling Series
e: By the mid-19th century, Richard M. Hoe of New York had perfected the power-driven cylindrical press, capable of printing 8,000 sheets per hour—particularly useful for printing newspapers.

q: Why was James Augustus Hickey persecuted by Governor-General Warren Hastings in the 1780s?
o: Because Hickey published a lot of gossip about the East India Company's senior officials in India alongside advertisements
Because Hickey printed books in Sanskrit only
Because Hickey supported Tipu Sultan's army directly
Because Hickey refused to sell advertisements
e: Hickey published advertisements (including slave sales) AND gossip about the Company's senior officials in India; enraged by this, Governor-General Warren Hastings persecuted Hickey and encouraged officially sanctioned newspapers to counter damage to colonial image.

q: Which two famous printing presses in 19th-century North and West India published numerous religious texts in vernacular languages?
o: Naval Kishore Press at Lucknow and Shri Venkateshwar Press in Bombay
Gutenberg Press in Goa and Hickey Press in London
Deoband Press in Madras and Serampore in Goa
British Museum Press and Paris Press
e: From the 1880s, the Naval Kishore Press at Lucknow and the Shri Venkateshwar Press in Bombay published numerous religious texts in vernaculars in portable, cheap forms.

q: Which Bengali writer wrote in the 1860s highlighting the experiences of women—how women were imprisoned at home, kept in ignorance, forced to do hard domestic labour and treated unjustly?
o: Kailashbashini Debi
Rashsundari Debi
Begum Rokeya
Tarabai Shinde
e: From the 1860s, a few Bengali women like Kailashbashini Debi wrote books highlighting the experiences of women—about how women were imprisoned at home, kept in ignorance, forced to do hard domestic labour and treated unjustly.

q: What was "Battala" in late 19th-century Calcutta?
o: An entire area in central Calcutta devoted to the printing of popular cheap books, illustrated profusely with woodcuts and coloured lithographs
The British Governor's private palace
A port for shipping opium to China
An exclusive Sanskrit university
e: In Bengal, an entire area in central Calcutta — the Battala — was devoted to the printing of popular books (cheap religious tracts as well as controversial/scandalous literature illustrated with woodcuts and coloured lithographs), carried by pedlars to women's homes.

q: Who published the fast-selling Punjabi book "Istri Dharm Vichar" to teach women how to be obedient wives?
o: Ram Chaddha
Kashibaba
Bhai Vir Singh
Lala Lajpat Rai
e: In Punjab too, a similar folk literature was widely printed from the early 20th century: Ram Chaddha published the fast-selling Istri Dharm Vichar to teach women how to be obedient wives, alongside cheap booklets by the Khalsa Tract Society.

q: What was the name of the collection of poems written by a Kanpur millworker under the pen-name "Sudarshan Chakr" between 1935 and 1955?
o: Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal
Sacchi Kavitayan
Gulamgiri
Amar Jiban
e: Another Kanpur millworker, who wrote under the name of Sudarshan Chakr between 1935 and 1955, brought together and published a collection called Sacchi Kavitayan.

q: Who passed the 1835 press regulations restoring earlier press freedoms in British India after receiving petitions from newspaper editors?
o: Lord Lytton
Governor-General William Bentinck
Warren Hastings
Lord Curzon
e: In 1835, faced with urgent petitions by editors of English and vernacular newspapers, Governor-General Bentinck agreed to revise press laws, and Thomas Macaulay formulated new rules that restored the earlier freedoms.

q: What did the Latin scholar Erasmus fear about the explosion of printed books in early 16th-century Europe?
o: He feared the multitude of new books—many ignorant, slanderous, irreligious and seditious—would hurt genuine scholarship and lower the value even of good books
He complained books were too expensive
He feared all paper supplies would run out in China
He wanted only Chapbooks to be sold
e: Erasmus, a Latin scholar and Catholic reformer, expressed deep anxiety about printing in Adages (1508), lamenting that the "swarm of new books" contained hurtful, stupid, ignorant and slanderous writings that cheapened even valuable books.

q: When were children's presses dedicated exclusively to literature for children first set up in Europe?
o: In France in 1857
In Italy in 1457
In India in 1757
In Spain in 1927
e: As primary education became compulsory from the late 19th century, children became an important category of readers; a children's press, devoted to literature for children alone, was set up in France in 1857.

q: Which famous women novelists of 19th-century Europe helped define a new type of woman—a person with will, strength of personality, determination and the power to think?
o: Jane Austen, the Brontë sisters and George Eliot
Rashsundari Debi and Tarabai Shinde
Queen Elizabeth and Mary Shelley only
Grimm Brothers
e: Some of the best-known novelists in the 19th century were women: Jane Austen, the Brontë sisters and George Eliot, whose writings redefined woman as a person with will, strength of personality, determination and thought.

q: When was the "Offset Press", capable of printing up to six colours at a time, developed?
o: Mid-15th century
Late 19th century
17th century
Mid-16th century
e: In the late 19th century, the offset press was developed which could print up to six colours at a time, followed by electrically operated presses from the turn of the 20th century.

q: What was the publisher strategy used in Britain during the 1930s Great Depression to sustain book purchases when consumer incomes dropped?
o: They brought out cheap paperback editions (after the 1920s Shilling Series)
They raised book prices by 500%
They printed books only on vellum
They banned all lending libraries
e: In the 1920s in England, popular works were sold in cheap series called the Shilling Series, and with the onset of the Great Depression in the 1930s publishers brought out cheap paperback editions to sustain buying.

q: Which traditional Indian material was used to copy handwritten manuscripts before the age of print?
o: Palm leaves (ताड़ के पत्तों) or handmade paper
Papyrus reeds from Rome only
Steel plates only
Plastics and linen cloths
e: India had a very rich and old tradition of handwritten manuscripts in Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian and vernaculars, copied on palm leaves or on handmade paper, often beautifully illustrated and bound between wooden covers.

q: Why were pre-print manuscripts NOT widely used in everyday life in pre-colonial India?
o: Because manuscripts were highly expensive and fragile, had to be handled carefully, and could not be read easily as scripts were written in different styles
Because Indians disliked literature
Because there were no languages in India before 1800
Because the British confiscated all palm leaves in 1500
e: Manuscripts were highly expensive and fragile, had to be handled carefully, and were difficult to read because different styles of scripts were used; thus they were not widely used in everyday life.

q: In 1867–1900s India, which painter produced mythological prints at the Ravi Varma Press for mass circulation?
o: Abanindranath Tagore
Raja Ravi Varma
Nandalal Bose
Amrita Sher-Gil
e: By the end of the 19th century, a new visual culture was taking shape; painters like Raja Ravi Varma produced images for mass circulation, and woodblocks/cheap prints could be bought by even the poor to decorate homes.

q: Which leader's statement in 1926 strongly condemned men for withholding education from women in the name of religion?
o: Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossein
Rashsundari Debi
Pandita Ramabai
Sarojini Naidu
e: In 1926, Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossein, a noted educationist and literary figure, strongly condemned men for withholding education from women in the name of religion as she addressed the Bengal Women's Education Conference (NCERT Box 3).

q: Who was the 20th-century Tamil social reformer who wrote powerfully on caste in the Madras Presidency?
o: E. V. Ramaswamy Naicker (Periyar)
Natesa Sastri
Subramania Bharati
C. Rajagopalachari
e: In the 20th century, B. R. Ambedkar in Maharashtra and E. V. Ramaswamy Naicker in Madras, better known as Periyar, wrote powerfully on caste and their writings were read by people all over India.

q: What was Mahatma Gandhi's 1922 observation about the "liberty of speech, liberty of the press, and freedom of association"?
o: He said the fight for Swaraj, for Khilafat, means a fight for this threatened freedom before all else, as these three are the most powerful vehicles of expressing public opinion
He called all three unnecessary luxuries
He supported the Vernacular Press Act
He banned newspapers during NCM
e: In 1922, Gandhi declared that the Government of India was trying to crush the three most powerful vehicles of expressing public opinion: liberty of speech, liberty of the press, and freedom of association — making the fight for Swaraj a fight for these freedoms before all else (NCERT Box 5).

q: What did the Bangalore cotton millworkers do in the 1930s following the example of Bombay millworkers?
o: They set up libraries to educate themselves, sponsored by social reformers trying to restrict excessive drinking, bring literacy and propagate nationalism
They burnt down all libraries in Karnataka
They stopped reading vernacular books
They only studied Greek in factories
e: By the 1930s, Bangalore cotton millworkers set up libraries to educate themselves, following the example of Bombay workers, sponsored by social reformers to restrict drinking, bring literacy and sometimes propagate nationalism.

q: Why was the book "diamond sutra" and earlier Buddhist missionaries from China significant in Japan around AD 768–770?
o: They introduced hand-printing technology into Japan
They built the first offset rotary cylinder in Edo
They brought European movable metal type to Kyoto
They outlawed Japanese poetry
e: Buddhist missionaries from China introduced hand-printing technology into Japan around AD 768–770, leading to the Diamond Sutra in AD 868.

q: Why were European booksellers forced to hire large numbers of scribes before mechanical printing arrived?
o: Booksellers employed large numbers of scribes (कातिब/सुलेखक) to copy manuscripts faster; over 50 scribes often worked for a single bookseller
Booksellers immediately invented computers
Monasteries banned all books completely
Students copied only on bamboo strips
e: To satisfy the expanding demand for books before mechanical printing, booksellers all over Europe exported books and organised book fairs, and increasingly employed skilled scribes — often over 50 scribes worked for a single bookseller.

q: Under the Vernacular Press Act of 1878, what happened if a vernacular newspaper published anything judged "seditious"?
o: The newspaper was warned first, and if it ignored the warning, the press was liable to be seized and the printing machinery confiscated
Its editor was awarded a medal in London
The British government paid double advertisement subsidies
It was allowed to continue after paying Rs 1 fine
e: Under the Vernacular Press Act (1878), the government kept regular track of vernacular newspapers; when a report was judged seditious, the newspaper was warned, and if ignored, the press could be seized and printing machinery confiscated.

q: In 16th–17th century Japan, what materials besides books were commonly printed on woodblocks in urban Edo and Kyoto?
o: Textiles, playing cards and paper money
Plastic bottles and vinyl records
Steel beams and steam boilers
Glass windows
e: In medieval Japan, poets and prose writers were regularly published, and printing of visual material led to interesting publishing practices where textiles, playing cards and paper money were commonly printed.

q: Which 19th-century Indian social and religious debate intensified because printed tracts and newspapers were published in spoken everyday languages?
o: Printed tracts not only spread new ideas but also shaped the nature of debate, enabling a wider public (including non-scholars) to participate in public discussions and express their views
Only British officials in London could read Indian religious tracts
Debates stopped completely in Bengal and North India
All temples banned paper books
e: From the early 19th century there were intense debates around religious issues (widow immolation, monotheism, Brahmanical priesthood, idolatry); printed tracts and newspapers in everyday spoken Bengali/Hindi/Persian enabled a wider public to participate in shaping new ideas.

q: Why did the production of handwritten manuscripts fail to satisfy the ever-increasing demand for books in 15th-century Europe?
o: Copying was an expensive, laborious and time-consuming business; manuscripts were fragile, awkward to handle and could not be carried around or read easily
Because European scribes went on a permanent strike in 1400
Because vellum stopped existing worldwide
Because churches burned every library
e: Even with 50+ scribes employed per bookseller, hand copying could not meet surging European demand because manuscripts were expensive, laborious, time-consuming, fragile and awkward to handle — creating urgent need for cheaper, quicker mechanical printing.

q: How did the Gutenberg press retain individual craftsmen's touch even while introducing mechanical mass production?
o: Spaces were left blank on printed pages for buyers to have individual painters add colour illumination and designs according to personal choice, so no two copies were identical
Every page was actually carved on stone
Paper sheets were painted completely black
Only two copies were ever printed
e: In books printed for the rich, blank spaces were left for decoration on the printed page; each purchaser could choose the design and decide on the painting school to do the illustrations, giving elites pride in unique copies.

q: What does NCERT describe as "a new reading public" merging with an older "hearing public" in early modern Europe?
o: Since literacy rates were still low, printers published profusely illustrated ballads and folk tales which could be sung and recited aloud in taverns and village gatherings, blurring the line between oral and reading cultures
Printers forced every peasant to pass a university degree before buying a book
Radio broadcasts replaced all printed books in 1550
Silent libraries banned folk songs
e: Earlier common people lived in an oral "hearing culture"; with printing, books reached wider sections, and to reach non-literate audiences printers published illustrated ballads and folk tales meant to be read aloud and sung—intermingling oral and print cultures.

q: What was the role of "Print Culture" in bringing about the Protestant Reformation according to historians?
o: Martin Luther's 1517 Ninety-Five Theses were immediately reproduced in vast numbers and read widely; his German translation of the New Testament sold 5,000 copies within weeks, creating an intellectual atmosphere that spread new ideas and led to a division in the Church
Print banned Luther's books permanently in 1517
Rome bought all printing presses in Germany
Luther used only hand-copied palm leaves
e: Print created the conditions for rapid circulation of Luther's Ninety-Five Theses (1517) and his New Testament translation (5,000 copies sold in weeks, 2nd edition in 3 months), directly aiding the Protestant Reformation.

q: How did print culture help create the conditions within which the French Revolution (1789) occurred, while not directly determining people's thoughts?
o: Print popularised Enlightenment thinkers' ideas (Voltaire, Rousseau), created a new culture of public dialogue and debate challenging tradition, and mocked the monarchy's morality via 1780s cartoons/literature—yet people still interpreted what they read alongside loyalist Church propaganda
Printing presses directly distributed weapons to every French peasant
Rousseau became the King of France in 1780
Print forbade any mention of taxes or monarchy
e: NCERT presents three arguments linking print and the French Revolution while adding the key nuance: print did not directly shape minds, because both critical Enlightenment texts and monarchical/Church propaganda existed side-by-side—print merely opened up the possibility of thinking differently.

q:
Arrange the following milestones in the history of Print in chronological order:
I. Printing press arrives in Goa
II. Gutenberg prints the Bible
III. Diamond Sutra printed in Japan
IV. Hickey starts Bengal Gazette
o: III → II → I → IV
II → III → I → IV
III → I → II → IV
I → II → III → IV
e: Diamond Sutra (AD 868) → Gutenberg Bible (~1448) → Printing press in Goa (mid-16th century / 1556) → Hickey's Bengal Gazette (1780).

q: Why were British-born conservative Hindus and orthodox Muslim families initially suspicious of women learning to read in 19th-century India?
o: Conservative Hindus believed a literate girl would be widowed, while conservative Muslims feared educated women would be corrupted by reading Urdu romances
Because women had no eyesight for reading
Because books were taxed 500% exclusively for women
Because English schools taught only gymnastics
e: NCERT notes these exact twin superstitions/fears in conservative 19th-century households, which brave women like Rashsundari Debi (secretly learning in her kitchen) and a north Indian Muslim girl (secretly learning Urdu) defied.

q: How did the arrival of print change the practice of reading religious texts like Tulsidas's "Ramcharitmanas" in 19th-century India?
o: Printed vernacular texts became cheap, portable and widely accessible, so they could be read easily at any place and time by ordinary people or read aloud to large groups of illiterate men and women
People stopped reading religious texts completely
Only priests in Goa were permitted to hold printed versions
Tulsidas wrote a second sequel in 1810
e: From 1810 onwards (and especially via Naval Kishore Press & Shri Venkateshwar Press from the 1880s), cheap portable vernacular religious editions reached a very wide public and could also be read out to large groups of illiterate people.

q:
Match the following authors/publishers with their famous works:
(i) Rashsundari Debi (ii) Jyotiba Phule (iii) Kashibaba (iv) Rammohun Roy
o: (i)-Amar Jiban, (ii)-Gulamgiri, (iii)-Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal, (iv)-Sambad Kaumudi
(i)-Gulamgiri, (ii)-Amar Jiban, (iii)-Sambad Kaumudi, (iv)-Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal
(i)-Sambad Kaumudi, (ii)-Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal, (iii)-Amar Jiban, (iv)-Gulamgiri
(i)-Kesari, (ii)-Bengal Gazette, (iii)-Sacchi Kavitayan, (iv)-Istri Dharm Vichar
e: Rashsundari Debi wrote Amar Jiban (1876); Jyotiba Phule wrote Gulamgiri (1871); Kashibaba wrote Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal (1938); Rammohun Roy published Sambad Kaumudi (1821).

q: Why did the British attitude toward press freedom in India change dramatically after the Revolt of 1857?
o: Enraged Englishmen demanded a clampdown on the "native" press because vernacular newspapers became assertively nationalist, leading to the 1878 Vernacular Press Act
Because the British discovered printing presses in Goa in 1858
Because English newspapers went completely silent
Because Indian newspapers praised British taxation

It provided the government with extensive rights to censor reports and editorials in the vernacular press." Why did the colonial government specifically target "vernacular" newspapers rather than English-owned papers?
o: Because Indian-language newspapers had become assertively nationalist and reached wide local Indian readerships, alarming colonial officials after 1857
Because Indian newspapers did not sell advertisements
Because English newspapers printed only in Chinese
Because Thomas Macaulay advised banning Hindi in 1878
e: After 1857, as vernacular newspapers grew assertively nationalist across India, the colonial government sought to silence native criticism via the 1878 Vernacular Press Act.

q: Case Study: "Despite repressive measures after 1878, nationalist newspapers grew in numbers in all parts of India. They reported on colonial misrule and encouraged nationalist activities." What happened in 1908 when Balgangadhar Tilak was imprisoned for writing in "Kesari"?
o: It provoked widespread protests all over India
All Indian editors immediately resigned and supported the Act
Kesari switched into Portuguese language
Tilak stayed silent and closed the newspaper permanently
e: Attempts to throttle nationalist criticism provoked militant protest; when Balgangadhar Tilak was imprisoned in 1908 for writing sympathetically about deported Punjab revolutionaries in Kesari, this led to widespread protests all over India.

q:
Consider the following statements about early print in East Asia:
1. From AD 594 onwards, books in China were printed by rubbing paper against the inked surface of woodblocks.
2. Buddhist missionaries from China introduced hand-printing technology into Japan around AD 768–770.
3. The Japanese Diamond Sutra was printed in 1448.
Which of these statements are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
e: Statements 1 and 2 are exact NCERT dates (AD 594 China; AD 768–770 Japan). Statement 3 is incorrect because the Diamond Sutra was printed in AD 868 (1448 was Gutenberg's Bible!).

q: Why was woodblock printing NOT invented in Europe before 1295, and why did Gutenberg's movable metal type succeed better for European languages than East Asian scripts?
o: European alphabets have only ~26 Roman letters that could be rearranged infinitely on metal type, whereas Chinese script has thousands of distinct logographic characters requiring separate carved blocks
Chinese paper could not absorb European oil ink
European wood could not be carved at all
Gutenberg invented paper first in 1430
e: In Europe's phonetic 26-letter alphabet, Gutenberg devised metal types for each of the 26 Roman letters and moved them around to compose different words rapidly, revolutionising printing far faster than woodblocks.

q: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched regarding European print personalities?
o: Erasmus — Latin scholar & Catholic reformer who feared "swarm of new books" in Adages (1508)
Menocchio — Italian miller executed by the Inquisition for reinterpreting the Bible
Louise-Sebastien Mercier — French novelist declaring the printing press "the most powerful engine of progress"
Richard M. Hoe — Inventor of the traditional Japanese ukiyo woodcut print in 1753
e: Richard M. Hoe of New York perfected the power-driven cylindrical press in the mid-19th century (8,000 sheets/hr), whereas Japanese ukiyo woodblock prints of 1753–late 18th century were pioneered by Kitagawa Utamaro.

q: Why does NCERT say "Fear of Print" existed simultaneously among the Catholic Church, monarchs, and even Hindu/Muslim orthodoxy in 19th-century India?
o: Because uncontrolled access to printed books allowed ordinary people, women and lower castes to read and interpret scriptures/politics independently without relying on priests, censors or patriarchs
Because ink poisoned the air inside libraries
Because priests wanted newspapers to charge higher subscription fees
Because books were written only by foreign tourists
e: Whether the Catholic Inquisition punishing Menocchio, European monarchs censoring sedition, or conservative Indian households fearing female/lower-caste literacy, authorities feared print enabled independent questioning and threatened traditional control.

q:
Read this passage about Indian censorship:
"By the 1820s, the Calcutta Supreme Court passed certain regulations to control press freedom... In 1835, Governor-General Bentinck agreed to revise press laws."
Who formulated those 1835 liberal rules, and what 1878 law completely reversed that tolerance?
o: Thomas Macaulay formulated the 1835 rules restoring freedom; the Vernacular Press Act (1878) reversed it after 1857
Warren Hastings in 1835; Rowlatt Act in 1878
James Hickey in 1835; Inland Emigration Act in 1878
Charles Wood in 1835; Act of Union in 1878
e: Thomas Macaulay formulated new rules in 1835 restoring earlier press freedoms; however, post-1857 resentment among British officials culminated in the repressive Vernacular Press Act of 1878.

q: How did the late 18th-century Japanese urban culture in Edo (Tokyo) transform print from purely religious texts into popular entertainment?
o: Libraries and bookstores packed with hand-printed material on diverse subjects—women, musical instruments, calculations, tea ceremony, flower arrangements, proper etiquette, cooking and famous places—alongside ukiyo woodblock prints by Utamaro published by Tsutaya Juzaburo
Japanese bookstores were strictly limited to Buddhist scrolls
Edo used steam presses imported from New York in 1753
Reading was forbidden to women and merchants in Kyoto
e: In flourishing urban circles at Edo, illustrated collections of paintings depicted elegant urban culture (artists, courtesans, teahouse gatherings), while libraries and bookstores overflowed with practical books on etiquette, cooking, music, and ukiyo prints.

q: Why did British Indian authorities in 1780 feel compelled to encourage "officially sanctioned newspapers" after persecuting James Augustus Hickey?
o: To counter the flow of information from independent papers like Hickey's Bengal Gazette that published gossip about Company officials and damaged the image of the colonial government
Because official newspapers were written only in Sanskrit
Because Britain wanted Indian nationalists to criticise Hastings freely
Because the East India Company lacked paper mills
e: Governor-General Warren Hastings persecuted Hickey and actively encouraged the publication of officially sanctioned newspapers that could counter the flow of information damaging the image of the colonial government.

q: Which statement accurately compares print's influence on 19th-century European women vs 19th-century Indian women?
o: In both Europe and India, women's reading expanded dramatically and manuals on proper domestic behaviour coexisted with radical female authors (Austen/Eliot/Brontës in Europe; Rashsundari Debi/Kailashbashini/Tarabai Shinde/Pandita Ramabai in India) challenging domestic confinement
Only European women ever wrote books in the 19th century
In India, printing was legally forbidden to women until 1947
European penny magazines prohibited women from reading
e: Notice the rich NCERT parallel: both Europe (penny magazines & Austen/Brontë/Eliot) and India (home-tutoring/orthodox backlash & Rashsundari Debi/Kailashbashini/Tarabai Shinde/Pandita Ramabai/Begum Rokeya/Ram Chaddha) experienced fierce debates over women's education and empowerment through print.

q:
Consider the following statements about 19th-century Indian religious print debates:
1. Religious sects feared colonial conversions so they used print to explain their own scriptures and counter missionary/rival arguments.
2. Every religious community printed strictly in Sanskrit or Arabic only, never in spoken vernaculars.
3. Even among illiterate people, vernacular religious prints were widely heard in public readings.
Which of the above statements are correct?
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
e: Statements 1 and 3 are true. Statement 2 is false because the central power of 19th-century Indian print was precisely that tracts and translations (Hindi, Bengali, Urdu, Tamil, Gujarati) were printed in everyday spoken languages!

q: Why was the "Bibliothèque Bleue" in France compared with English "Chapbooks" in 18th-century Europe?
o: Both were very cheap, small-format popular books printed on low-cost paper specifically designed to reach poor and newly literate common readers beyond the wealthy elite
Both were expensive Latin Bibles locked in monasteries
Both were published exclusively by the Vatican Inquisition
Both were written by Isaac Newton
e: Penny chapbooks in England (sold by chapmen for a penny) and Bibliothèque Bleue in France (low-priced small books in cheap blue covers) both enabled the European poor and common folk to buy and read books during the 18th-century reading mania.

q: Why did some publishers in 19th-century Europe serialise important novels in periodicals before publishing them as full books?
o: Periodicals serialised important novels, which gave birth to a particular way of writing novels while making reading affordable and sustaining regular reader suspense and subscriptions
Because ink dried only once a year
Because full books were banned by law until 1920
Only for university professors in Rome
e: NCERT notes that periodicals serialised important novels in the 19th century, which gave birth to a particular way of writing novels and expanded readership across classes.

q: What was "Lending Libraries" and "20th-century Dust Cover / Book Jacket" in the history of print marketing?
o: Both were 20th-century marketing innovations: the Shilling Series in 1920s England and the dust cover (book jacket) in the 20th century, alongside cheap paperbacks in the 1930s Great Depression
Both were invented in 1295 China by Marco Polo
Both were banned by the 1558 Roman Index
Both were exclusive to palm-leaf manuscripts
e: Printers and publishers continuously developed new strategies to sell their product: 19th-century periodicals serialised novels, 1920s England sold popular works in the Shilling Series, the dust cover / book jacket was a 20th-century innovation, and 1930s Great Depression saw cheap paperbacks.

q: Which European movement does Martin Luther's famous quote ("Printing is the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one") directly refer to?
o: The Protestant Reformation triggered in 1517 when Luther's Ninety-Five Theses and translated New Testament spread rapidly through print
The French Revolution of 1789
The 1848 Frankfurt Parliament
The 1885 Berlin Conference
e: Deeply grateful to print for rapidly spreading his ideas against Catholic Church practices (selling 5,000 copies of his German New Testament in weeks), Martin Luther hailed printing as God's greatest gift, anchoring the Protestant Reformation.

q: What did the "Battala" woodcuts and cheap lithographs sold in late 19th-century Calcutta accomplish socially?
o: Pedlars took Battala publications right to homes, enabling middle-class and ordinary women to read books in their leisure time and making popular reading accessible beyond wealthy elites
They banned women from reading novels
They forced all Bengali readers to learn Latin
They ended printing in Bombay
e: Battala publications (religious tracts, scandalous literature, calendars, illustrated prints) were carried by pedlars right to homes, enabling women to read them in their leisure time.

q:
Read the two statements about 19th-century Japanese & Chinese print:
Statement I: By the 17th century, as urban culture bloomed in China, reading increasingly became a leisure activity.
Statement II: In late 18th-century Edo (Tokyo), flourished illustrated print collections called "ukiyo" depicting artists, courtesans and teahouse gatherings.
Which is true?
o: Only Statement I
Only Statement II
Both Statements I and II
Neither Statement I nor II
e: Both statements are directly taken from NCERT Section 1 ("The First Printed Books" and "Print in Japan").

q: How did the spread of print in India create a "pan-Indian identity" even across different linguistic communities in the 19th century?
o: Newspapers conveyed news from one place to another, connecting different communities and regions across India and enabling common debates on social reform, caste and colonial rule
Because every newspaper in India used only French
Because Warren Hastings banned regional news permanently
Because telegraph lines were forbidden for newspapers
e: NCERT explains that while print triggered religious/regional controversies, newspapers also conveyed news from one place to another, creating pan-Indian identities.

q: Why was Richard M. Hoe's power-driven cylindrical press (8,000 sheets/hr) particularly revolutionary for newspapers compared to Gutenberg's flatbed screw press (250 sheets/hr)?
o: Daily newspaper publishing, which required printing tens of thousands of fresh copies within a few hours before morning distribution
Hand-illuminated medieval church Latin Bibles
Palm-leaf transcription in Goa
Stone carving in ancient China
e: Increasing the output 32-fold from 250 sheets/hr to 8,000 sheets/hr made the power-driven cylindrical press "particularly useful for printing newspapers" (NCERT Section 5.2).

q: What was "Ulama" and "Fatwa" in the context of 19th-century North Indian print debates?
o: Ulama are legal scholars of Islam and the sharia; a Fatwa is a legal pronouncement on Islamic law usually given by a mufti (legal scholar) to clarify questions
Ulama were Portuguese Jesuit priests; Fatwa was a colonial press tax
Ulama were Marathi cotton workers; Fatwa was a play
Ulama were European publishers; Fatwa was a Chapbook
e: NCERT Box / Glossary defines Ulama as legal scholars of Islam and the sharia, and Fatwa as a legal pronouncement on Islamic law usually given by a mufti to clarify issues where the law is uncertain.

q: Why was Mahatma Gandhi's 1922 editorial defending "liberty of speech, liberty of the press, and freedom of association" critical during British rule?
o: Because wartime Defence of India Rules (1914–18) and the 1919 Rowlatt Act sought to suppress all nationalist reports and public mobilisation, making civil liberties the very core of the Swaraj struggle
Because Gandhi wanted to reinstate the 1878 Vernacular Press Act
Because all Indian newspapers were run by the East India Company in 1922
Because Gandhi opposed public speech
e: During WWI (Defence of India Rules) and 1919 (Rowlatt Act), the colonial government forced newspapers to shut down or furnish securities; Gandhi responded in 1922 by declaring the fight for Swaraj was above all a fight for these three threatened freedoms.

q: Which of the following correctly captures the transformation from "hand printing in China" to "mass-market paperback editions in the 1930s"?
o: Chinese woodblock & accordion books → Korean/Japanese hand printing → European manuscript/vellum era → Gutenberg's movable metal type (1448) → Reading mania chapbooks (18th c.) → Cylinder & Offset presses (19th c.) → Cheap paperbacks (1930s)
Offset press → Chinese woodblock → Gutenberg Bible → Diamond Sutra
Gutenberg Bible → Diamond Sutra → Accordion books → Vellum manuscripts
Chapbooks → Palm leaves → Gutenberg → Cylindrical press
e: This sequence faithfully traces the entire multi-century global trajectory of print culture from AD 594 China and AD 868 Japan through 1448 Europe to 19th–20th-century industrial mass publishing.

q: Why did the French writer Voltaire and philosopher Jean Jacques Rousseau become symbols of pre-revolutionary print debate even though peasants largely remained non-literate?
o: Printed ideas spread through public reading aloud in salons, coffee-houses, taverns and pamphlets/caricatures that discussed Enlightenment principles of reason and questioned Church/despotic authority
Voltaire invented television broadcasts in Paris
Every French peasant held a doctorate degree in Latin
King Louis XVI translated Rousseau for free distribution
e: Thinkers like Voltaire and Rousseau attacked the sacred authority of the Church and despotic power of the state; ideas of science, reason and rationality reached the wider public via coffee-houses, salons, pamphlets and public debates.

q:
Which pair of statements correctly describes early European censorship vs colonial Indian censorship?
1. The Roman Catholic Church maintained the Index of Prohibited Books from 1558.
2. The British government in India passed the Vernacular Press Act in 1878 modelled on Irish Press Laws.
3. Neither the Roman Church nor the British government ever confiscated a printing press.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
e: Statements 1 and 2 are accurate NCERT facts. Statement 3 is false because the Roman Church strictly punished heretics/booksellers and the 1878 Vernacular Press Act explicitly authorised seizure of presses and confiscation of printing machinery.

q:
Compare how early print in China differed in purpose from early print in Europe (1450s):
Which statement captures this contrast accurately?
o: In China, the imperial state was the chief sponsor printing civil service exam textbooks on woodblocks; in Europe, commercial printers like Gutenberg using movable metal type quickly expanded Bibles, pamphlets, ballads and Reformation debates
In China printing was used only for novels, never examinations
In Europe Gutenberg printed exclusively imperial tax exams
Both China and Europe used offset presses from AD 600
e: In imperial China the state initially sponsored woodblock exam textbooks before urban commercial leisure reading grew in the 17th century; in Europe private presses rapidly commercialised movable type and ignited theological debates like Luther's 1517 theses.

q: Why did many Indian orthodox religious leaders and reformers BOTH embrace print during the 19th century instead of one side rejecting it?
o: Because any group wishing to shape public opinion in a debate had to answer printed arguments in print itself—so Rammohun Roy's Sambad Kaumudi was countered by orthodox Samachar Chandrika, and missionary/Hindu tracts were answered by ulama lithographs
Because the British fined anyone who rejected printing presses
Because manuscripts cost Rs 1 crore each
Because Sanskrit could not be handwritten
e: Printed tracts and newspapers did not favour just one side: once debates over sati, idolatry, monotheism and Islamic doctrine entered print, every faction (reformist and orthodox alike) needed print to reach the wider public.

q: Which of the following is an INCORRECT statement about early Indian press history?
o: The first printing press came to Goa with Portuguese missionaries in the mid-16th century
Catholic priests printed the first Tamil book at Cochin in 1579 and first Malayalam book in 1713
James Augustus Hickey's Bengal Gazette (1780) was praised and funded by Governor-General Warren Hastings
Gangadhar Bhattacharya brought out the first Indian weekly Bengal Gazette
e: Statement 3 is false: Governor-General Warren Hastings was ENRAGED by Hickey publishing gossip about Company officials, so Hastings persecuted Hickey and encouraged rival officially sanctioned newspapers instead.

q:
Read the three statements regarding 19th-century Indian women and print:
1. Kailashbashini Debi wrote in the 1860s about how women were imprisoned at home and kept in ignorance.
2. Pandita Ramabai and Tarabai Shinde wrote in the 1880s about the miserable lives of upper-caste Hindu widows in Maharashtra.
3. Ram Chaddha published Istri Dharm Vichar in Bengal to demand equal voting rights for women.
Which statements are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
e: Statements 1 and 2 are accurate NCERT facts. Statement 3 has two errors: Ram Chaddha published Istri Dharm Vichar in PUNJAB (not Bengal), and it was meant to teach women how to be "obedient wives" (conservative domestic ideal), NOT voting rights.

q: Why was "Martin Luther's translation of the New Testament" considered a milestone in print history rather than merely a religious text?
o: Selling 5,000 copies in a few weeks and needing a second edition within three months showed print's unprecedented speed in mobilising public opinion across ordinary readers in spoken vernacular German
Because it was written on palm leaves in Rome
Because the Pope personally printed it in Goa
Because it took 100 years to sell 180 copies
e: Print rapidly reproduced Luther's ideas in accessible vernacular language, selling 5,000 copies within weeks and sparking Europe's Protestant Reformation.

q: What was "Inquisition" and why was it linked with the 1558 Index of Prohibited Books in Europe?
o: The Inquisition was a former Roman Catholic court for identifying and punishing heretics; alarmed by individual Bible readings like Menocchio's, the Church used both Inquisition trials and the 1558 Index to control booksellers and suppress heretical ideas
It was a European association of paperback publishers
It was Martin Luther's German printing press
It was a trade union of Paris scribes
e: NCERT defines the Inquisition as a former Roman Catholic court for identifying and punishing heretics; after executing Menocchio twice brought before it, the Roman Church maintained the Index of Prohibited Books from 1558.

q: Which of the following combinations of Indian caste-and-class print pioneers in NCERT is COMPLETELY accurate?
o: Jyotiba Phule: Gulamgiri (1871) | Kashibaba: Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal (1938) | Sudarshan Chakr: Sacchi Kavitayan (1935–55)
Periyar: Amar Jiban | Jyotiba Phule: Kesari | Kashibaba: Sambad Kaumudi
B. R. Ambedkar: Sacchi Kavitayan | Sudarshan Chakr: Gulamgiri | Ram Chaddha: Bengal Gazette
Rashsundari Debi: Gulamgiri | Rammohun Roy: Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal
e: Option 1 accurately matches all three figures, titles and years directly from Section 8.2 ("Print and the Poor People") of NCERT Chapter 5 (Print Culture).

q: Why does NCERT cite the example of the "North Indian Muslim girl who secretly learnt to read and write in Urdu" alongside Rashsundari Debi?
o: To show that despite orthodox resistance against women's education across religious communities in 19th-century India, women used print and literacy to claim independent thought and learn beyond rote Arabic Quran recitation
To prove Urdu was banned throughout North India
Because both women were sisters living in Goa
To show only British women could read Urdu
e: NCERT places these accounts side by side to show how print awakened women's aspirations across both Hindu and Muslim households: when told to read only Arabic Quran she couldn't understand, the Muslim girl insisted on secretly learning to read Urdu.
